ta-l1d46q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 46. Having treated what God's will is and its senses, Lombard treats its efficacy: first questions suggesting it is inefficacious, whether something he wills does not happen and whether something happens that he does not will, then (Dist. 47) that it is efficacious in all things. On the first he raises a doubt from two authorities and expounds them. On the second, whether sins happen by God's will, he sets out two opinions (that God wills evils to be or happen, and that he does not), their arguments, the second's replies and arguments (goods come from evils; the cause of man's becoming worse is not in God; evils do not happen with God as author, i.e. willing), and chooses that God does not will evils to happen. Four articles are announced: whether God wills all to be saved; whether it is good that evils happen; whether evil belongs to the perfection of the universe; and whether God wills evils to happen.
claims: God does not will evils to happen.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e143.summary: First argument that God wills all to be saved, from 1 Tim. 2:4, 'he wills all to be saved'.
claims: God wills all to be saved.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e149.summary: Second argument, against the reply that he wills it conditionally, not absolutely. A conditional will is imperfect, and nothing imperfect is attributed to God.
claims: Conditional will is imperfect.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e152.summary: Third argument. The will of one with charity imitates God's, and one with charity desires everyone's salvation.
claims: Charity desires all to be saved.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e156.summary: Fourth argument. Every agent by intention wills its work to attain its end, and man's end is eternal salvation, for which God created him.
claims: God wills creatures to attain their end.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e159.summary: Fifth argument. No one can be saved unless God wills to save him, so if God does not will to save everyone, salvation is not in everyone's power, and we are not punished or blamed for what is not in our power, so it would not be imputed to the unsaved, which is false.
claims: Otherwise the damned would be blameless.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e162.summary: Sed contra. Predestination is the purpose of having mercy (Augustine), so if God willed all saved, all would be predestined, and since not all are saved, someone predestined would not be saved.
claims: Not all are predestined.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e165.summary: Second sed contra. God's will is the first and highest cause of things (Dist. 45), and given the cause the effect follows, and not all are saved.
claims: God's will is efficacious.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e168.summary: Thomas's determination. With Damascene, will is twofold, antecedent and consequent, not by any diversity in the divine will but by different conditions of the thing willed. In each human one can consider his nature and his other circumstances, that he wills and prepares for salvation or resists and acts contrarily. Considering only nature, it is equally good that every human be saved, since all share human nature, and since every good is willed by God, God wills this, the antecedent will by which he wills all to be saved (Damascene), whose effect is the order of nature to the end of salvation and the means offered to all in common, natural and gratuitous, like natural powers and the precepts of the law. Considering all the person's circumstances, it is not good that all be saved: it is good that one who prepares and consents be saved by the bounty of divine grace, but not good that one unwilling and resisting be saved, since it is unjust. Since something relates to being willed by God as it relates to being good, God does not will this person, so considered, to be saved, but only the one willing and consenting, and this is the consequent will, which presupposes foreknowledge of works not as cause of the will but as reason of the thing willed (Dist. 45).
claims: By antecedent will God wills all to be saved, considering human nature; by consequent will he wills the salvation of those who consent.
The distinction is in the conditions of the thing willed, not in God's will.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e171.summary: Reply to the first argument. According to Damascene, the Apostle's words concern antecedent, not consequent, will. According to Augustine they concern consequent will, expounded two ways: as an accommodated distribution, all who are saved, as in the text; or as a distribution over kinds of individuals, since he predestined some of every condition of humans to life, not over every individual of the kinds.
claims: 1 Tim. 2:4 concerns antecedent will, or, with Augustine, all the saved or all kinds.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the second argument. Antecedent will can be called conditional, yet the imperfection is not on the side of the divine will but of the thing willed, which is not taken with all the circumstances required for right order to salvation.
claims: Antecedent will's imperfection lies in its object's consideration.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e178.summary: Reply to the third argument. One with charity desires eternal salvation for all absolutely, since the conditions by which someone is disordered from salvation are not subject to his knowledge, though they are to God's, so the judgement differs between the will of one with charity and God's consequent will.
claims: Charity wills absolutely because it does not know the conditions God knows.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e181.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A wise artisan wills his work to attain its end only according to the character of the end: if it has a disposition contrary to the form he intends to induce, he does not induce the form unless that indisposition is removed, as a builder does not will stones to fit into the house while their roughness remains; so too with God.
claims: God wills the end according to the disposition of the recipient.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e184.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The conditions by which a human is disordered from attaining the end, under which God does not will him saved, come from the human himself, so all that follows is imputed to him as fault.
claims: The conditions excluding salvation are from the human.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e196.summary: First argument that it is good that evils happen. True and good are convertible, and it is true that evils happen.
claims: True and good convert.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e199.summary: Second argument. Whatever is willed is good, since evil is outside will (Dionysius), and that evils happen is willed by one who does evil voluntarily.
claims: What is willed is good.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e202.summary: Third argument. The cause of good seems good, as cold does not cause heat, and evils' happening causes good, as a bad action causes a good passion and much else.
claims: Evils cause goods.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e206.summary: Fourth argument. Every just thing is good, and evils' happening is just, since every punishment is from God and just, and one sin is the punishment of another (Gregory; Rom. 1:24; Rev. 22:11).
claims: Sin can be punishment of sin.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e215.summary: Sed contra. Some evils, like sinful acts, have being in happening, so if their happening is good, their being is good, which no opinion grants.
claims: The being of sinful acts is their happening.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e218.summary: Second sed contra. Motion takes its species from its term (the Philosopher), and every happening terminates in the being of what happens, so since evil is not good, neither is its happening.
claims: Becoming is specified by its term.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e221.summary: Thomas's determination. The text gives two opinions that agree that evils are not good but disagree whether evils' happening or being is good, the second, which denies it, seeming truer, as Lombard says. Evil per se is not good but can be good per accidens, as joined in the universe to some good to which it has an accidental order, as a builder is white per accidens, art and whiteness coinciding in one subject; and since being or happening implies an order, including a composition, the first opinion said that evils' being or happening is good. This does not suffice, since as evil per se is not good, neither is the order of evil good in itself, since evil as such is disordered, and its disorder is its order, as being deprived is its being and negation its position, as in other privations. So evils' happening or being is evil, not good, since 'evils are', said absolutely, designates the composition of this privation with its subject, in which the character of goodness does not consist, as 'whiteness is', abstractly, signifies its order to its subject, since an accident's being is inhering. But the comparison of evil to the good God draws from it is signified by 'is' in 'evils are occasions of goods', so that evils are occasions of goods is good, but that evils are, simply, is not good.
claims: That evils happen is not good; that evils are occasions of good is good.
The order of evil to its subject is itself disorder.
concepts: per se vs. per accidens good

ta-l1d46q1-d1e224.summary: Reply to the first argument. Truth concerns things whose character is completed by the soul's operation and founded in reality (Dist. 19), and nothing prevents the soul's operation about an evil thing from being good and the concept of an evil thing being good in the soul, as non-being in reality is called being in the reasoning soul, like negations and privations (Commentator, Metaphysics 4). So arguing from the goodness of truth as completed in the soul's operation to the goodness of what is in reality commits the fallacy of accident; it is true that evils are, and this truth by which it is truly said that evils are is good, though evils' being is evil.
claims: The truth that evils exist is good; their existing is not.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e227.summary: Reply to the second argument. Evils' happening is willed not per se but per accidens, as estimated good by reason of some annexed good, since nothing is purely evil (Dionysius), so every evil person is in a way ignorant (the Philosopher), deceived in choosing.
claims: Evil is willed only under the appearance of good.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e231.summary: Reply to the third argument. Evils' happening causes good only occasionally and per accidens. Some accidental causes contribute nothing to the effect, as the builder's music to the house; some operate up to the effect but produce it beyond intention, chance or fortune, as digging a grave one finds treasure; and some operate but not up to the joined effect, and so evils' happening is an accidental cause of good, as the tyrant's persecution touches not the martyr's patience but the bodily torment that is its matter, and such a cause is properly called an occasion. So it does not follow that evils' happening is good, since one contrary can cause another per accidens, as cold heats per accidens (Physics 8).
claims: Evil is an occasion of good, not its cause.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e234.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Sin is not per se punishment, only per accidens, by reason of what precedes and follows it. The sinful act as from a voluntary agent has the character of fault and injustice, but what precedes it, desertion by God for the merit of prior fault, as from divine ordering, has the character of punishment and is just; and the defect following the sinful act, falling short of a great good while inordinately pursuing a small one, as one seeking bodily pleasure loses the delight of God, is a punishment from God's just ordering, so Augustine says every disordered mind is its own punishment.
claims: Sin is punishment only by what precedes (desertion) and follows (loss of the greater good).

ta-l1d46q1-d1e246.summary: First argument that evil belongs to the perfection of the universe. Dionysius says evil will contribute to the perfection of all (the universe) and give the whole not to be imperfect.
claims: Dionysius on evil and perfection.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e255.summary: Second argument. The universe's good is the good of order, and evil is ordered in the universe, as the text says evil well ordered and in its place commends goods more eminently.
claims: Ordered evil commends goods.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e258.summary: Third argument. What the universe would lack many perfections without contributes to its perfection, and without evil there would be no forms of mixtures (from elements' corruption), no martyrs' patience, no mercy without misery.
claims: Evil enables many perfections.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e262.summary: Fourth argument. Every character of goodness contributes to the universe's perfection, and without evil a character of goodness would be lacking, the goodness of comparison by which good is commended by contrast with evil.
claims: Evil gives goodness of comparison.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e265.summary: Sed contra. What belongs to the universe's perfection is either existent, like substance, or in existents, like accidents, and evil is neither (Dionysius).
claims: Evil is neither substance nor accident.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e268.summary: Second sed contra. What the universe would be better without does not contribute to its perfection, and without evil it would be better, since evil takes more from one than it adds to another: absolute goodness from its subject, goodness of comparison to another.
claims: Evil takes more than it gives.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e271.summary: Thomas's determination. Evil does not per se contribute to the universe's perfection, since what contributes per se is a constituent part or a per se cause of some perfection, and evil is not a part of the universe, being neither substance nor accident but only privation (Dionysius), nor per se causes any good. But it contributes per accidens, as joined to something belonging to the universe's perfection, either antecedent to evil, like a nature that sometimes fails and sometimes not, as human free choice, without which nature, from whose defect evil arises, the universe would not be perfect in all grades of goodness; or consequent to it, the good occasioned by evil, the beauty resulting for the good by comparison with evil, or a perfection to which evil relates materially, as persecution to patience, and in infinitely many other ways, since accidental causes are infinite (the Philosopher).
claims: Evil contributes to the universe's perfection only per accidens, through defectible natures and goods occasioned by it.
concepts: evil and the perfection of the universe

ta-l1d46q1-d1e274.summary: Reply to the first argument. Dionysius concludes this by reduction to the impossible, leaving as unfitting that evil per se belongs to the universe's perfection.
claims: Dionysius argues by reductio.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e277.summary: Reply to the second argument. The good of order by which evil is ordered is not in what has the evil but in another, as the tyrant's savagery is ordered by the martyr's patience, or in the same person now changed, as the habitual order resulting from prior sin in one made other by penance, since the just person orders his prior sin. So evil contributes to the universe's perfection only per accidens.
claims: The order of evil lies in another or in the converted person.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e281.summary: Reply to the third argument. Evil does not bring those perfections per se; they follow it per accidens.
claims: Perfections follow evil per accidens.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e284.summary: Likewise to the fourth argument. Even if there were no evil, there could be goodness of comparison between greater and lesser good, since the lesser good, though lacking some perfection of the greater, need not be evil, evil being privation of what is due and naturally had, like blindness.
claims: Comparison is possible between goods without evil.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e287.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. Dionysius means evil is not anything positive, either subsisting or existing in another, which shows it does not per se pertain to the universe's perfection, but nothing prevents its pertaining per accidens.
claims: Evil pertains per accidens.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e290.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Of all evils it is universally true that if they were not permitted the universe would be more imperfect, since the natures able to fail would not exist, and without them not all grades of goodness would be filled. Some evils, if absent, would make the universe more imperfect, those followed by a greater perfection than what they deprive, like the corruption of elements followed by mixture and the nobler forms of mixtures. Others, if absent, would make it more perfect, those depriving greater perfections than they produce in another, especially evils of fault, which deprive one of grace and glory and give another goodness of comparison or some perfection without which final perfection could still be had, as one can reach eternal life without the act of patience under persecution. So if no human had sinned, the human race would be better, since even if one's salvation is directly occasioned by another's fault, it could be attained without it; yet neither kind of evil per se makes for the universe's perfection, since they are occasions, not causes, of perfections.
claims: Permitting defectible natures perfects the universe; some evils yield greater goods, but evils of fault leave the world worse.
If no one had sinned, the human race would be better.
concepts: evils of fault vs. natural evils

ta-l1d46q1-d1e303.summary: First argument that God wills evils to happen. Seneca says the wise man is not disturbed but rejoices in misfortunes, where the good of his virtue appears, as the Philosopher suggests of the happy man, and God is wisest and happiest, and the beauty of his justice and wisdom appears in evils.
claims: The wise rejoice in misfortunes.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e306.summary: Second argument. Evils happening and not happening are contradictories, with no middle, and 'God wills evils not to happen' is commonly granted to be false, so 'God wills evils to happen' is true.
claims: Contradictories leave no middle.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e309.summary: Third argument. No wise person wills the impossible, and removing evils' not happening necessarily leaves their happening, and God does not will evils not to happen, so he necessarily wills them to happen.
claims: Not willing their not happening implies willing their happening.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e313.summary: Fourth argument. God is author of nature as of grace, and as fault deprives the good of grace, punishment deprives the good of nature (Augustine), and God wills the punishments of hell, so likewise evils of fault.
claims: God wills punishment, so fault too.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e316.summary: Sed contra. Will is only of the end and what is ordered to it, and evils happen only by disorder from the end.
claims: Evil is disorder from the end.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e319.summary: Second sed contra. Whoever conforms his will to God's does not sin, and every sinner sins by willing evils to be done by him, so he does not conform to God's will, so God does not will evils to happen.
claims: Sinners do not conform to God's will.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e322.summary: Thomas's determination. Since God's will is the cause of all goods and of all he wills, something relates to being willed by God as it relates to being good, so since evils' happening is not good in itself (previous article), it is not willed per se by God. But each good joined to it is good and willed by God: the antecedent good, the condition of a nature able to fail, which God established and conserves, so he does not will evils to happen but wills to permit evils to happen; and the consequent good by which evil is ordered, so he wills to order evils that have happened, not that they happen.
claims: God does not will evils to happen; he wills to permit them and to order them.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e325.summary: Reply to the first argument. The beauty of divine wisdom appears in the permitting and ordering of evils, both of which God wills, but not in evil's happening, which in itself is a departure from the beauty of the form of the first exemplar.
claims: God wills permission and ordering, not evil.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e328.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though evils happening and not happening are opposed by affirmation and negation, 'to will them to happen' and 'to will them not to happen' are not contradictories, both being affirmative with the act of will affirmed. So neither should be granted, but 'not to will them to happen', which is negative; in 'to will not to happen' the act of will remains affirmed and the negation bears on the thing willed, as in its whole declension, so 'to nill them to happen' is the same as 'to will them not to happen'.
claims: 'Willing evils to happen' and 'willing them not to happen' are contraries, not contradictories; God does neither.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e332.summary: Reply to the third argument. By antecedent will God wills evils of fault not to happen, but not by consequent will, except for those he knows will not will to do evils, since consequent will receives the creature's condition; yet it does not follow that by consequent will he wills evils to happen, but that he wills to permit them. Nor does he will the impossible, since he does not will evils both to happen and not happen, or neither. Evils happening and not happening are contradictories with no middle, but willing them to happen and willing them not to happen are not contradictories, so one need not be true.
claims: By consequent will God permits evils without willing them.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e335.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. As evil opposed to grace is not willed by God, neither is evil opposed to nature, but he wills the order of one to the other, which is implied in the character of punishment, so he wills punishment to be inflicted but not fault to happen, since fault signifies evil as coming from a defective cause, not as ordered by God.
claims: God wills punishment as ordering, not fault.

ta-l1d46q1-d1e344.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Not because no human is not enlightened, but because none is enlightened except by him' concerns the light of grace; the light of natural intellect enlightens every human absolutely, since every truth, by whomever said, is from the Holy Spirit (Ambrose). (2) The fourfold division of good: since good comes from one complete cause and evil from many particular defects (Dionysius), an act absolutely good requires goodness of object (like almsgiving) and goodness on the agent's side (will or choice, due end, and firmness, Ethics 2), and acts directed to another require also an effect of goodness in the recipient. So good in itself, to the doer, and to the recipient is good per se, simply, and perfectly; good in itself and to the doer, not the recipient, is simply good but not perfect; good in itself and to the recipient, not the doer, is good per se but not simply; good only to the recipient is good per accidens; good to the doer but not in itself is impossible; and nothing benefits none. (3) Augustine argues 'from the lesser', a negative topic: if no wise man makes a man worse, much less God; 'wise' means virtuous, from Socrates' view that virtues are sciences, true of ignorance in particular choice, or prudent, as the prudent does not sin. (4) The second argument differs, proceeding from goodness rather than divine authorship. (5) God is not the cause of tending to non-being, though he says 'I kill and make alive' (Deut. 32:39), since non-being is never intended per se but some being on which a non-being follows, as fire's being entails air's non-being; God wills the order of justice and nature, on which the corruption and punishment of some follow. (6) The evildoer tends to non-being, though evil corrupts no existent (Dionysius), since evil is privation, a kind of non-being, though some being always underlies it, so the sinner tends to the non-being of grace, not of nature.
claims: Natural light is from God for all; grace for some.
An act is fully good in object, agent, and effect.
God intends being; non-being follows incidentally from his order.

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 46 divides Lombard's questions about the efficacy of God's will (whether what he wills fails to happen, whether what he does not will happens) and his choice that God does not will evils. It announces four articles: universal salvific will, the goodness of evils' happening, evil and the universe's perfection, and whether God wills evils.
claims: God does not will evils to happen.

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e135.summary: Article 1 holds, with Damascene, that by antecedent will, considering human nature, God wills all to be saved, offering the means to all, while by consequent will, considering all circumstances, he wills the salvation only of those who consent, since saving the resisting would be unjust. The distinction lies in the conditions of the thing willed. 1 Tim. 2:4 can be read of antecedent will or, with Augustine, of all the saved or all kinds. Charity wills absolutely for lack of God's knowledge, and the conditions excluding salvation come from the human.
claims: God wills all to be saved antecedently and the consenting consequently.

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e188.summary: Article 2 holds that it is not good that evils happen, since the order of evil to its subject is itself disorder, though it is good that evils are occasions of good. The truth that evils exist is good, evil is willed only under the appearance of good, evil is an occasion and not a cause of good, and sin is punishment only by what precedes and follows it.
claims: Evils' happening is not good; their being occasions of good is.

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e238.summary: Article 3 holds that evil contributes to the universe's perfection only per accidens, through defectible natures (like free choice) that fill the grades of goodness and through goods occasioned by evil. Some evils yield greater goods, like elemental corruption, but evils of fault leave the world worse, and if no one had sinned the human race would be better.
claims: Evil perfects the universe only per accidens; sin makes it worse.
concepts: evil and the perfection of the universe

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e295.summary: Article 4 holds that God does not will evils to happen but wills to permit them, by willing defectible natures, and to order them, by willing the consequent good. 'Willing evils to happen' and 'willing them not to happen' are contraries, so God need do neither. By consequent will he permits evils, and he wills punishment as an ordering but not fault.
claims: God permits and orders evils without willing them.

ta-l1d46q1-Dd1e339.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 46 distinguishes natural light, given to all, from grace, given to some. It sets out a fourfold division of good, and explains that God intends being, non-being following only incidentally from his order of justice and nature.
claims: God intends being; natural light is from him for all.

ta-l1d46q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 46 treats God's will and evil. Article 1 distinguishes antecedent will, by which God wills all to be saved, from consequent will, by which he wills the salvation of those who consent. Article 2 holds that evils' happening is not good, though their being occasions of good is. Article 3 holds that evil contributes to the universe's perfection only per accidens, and that sin leaves the world worse. Article 4 holds that God does not will evils to happen but wills to permit and to order them.
claims: God wills all to be saved antecedently, the consenting consequently.
God permits and orders evils without willing them.
Evil perfects the universe only per accidens.
